Chose: A rebuild goes into a directory beside the first, and the old one is removed

where scip-go gomod github.com/hypertheory-labs/phoropter . `github.com/hypertheory-labs/phoropter/internal/site`/live#rebuild(). symbol page

quote dir := fmt.Sprintf("%s.rebuild-%d", l.o.Out, l.n)

Because (Claude, not asked): a fresh directory means no request reads a half-written site. Each one is removed once the next is swapped in, and a server starting up clears any left by one that was killed. A rebuild that fails leaves the last site up, says so on stderr, and isn't tried again until HEAD moves.

Answered: Following HEAD costs nothing a reader notices

Answers the plan’s guess: disproved.

Answer (Claude, measured): disproved, on both counts. On phoropter's repository (98 pages, indexes in the store), the first request after a commit took 5.9s, because it waits for the whole rebuild. Requests between commits went from under 1ms to about 20-25ms, which is the once-a-second git rev-parse. Nobody notices the second. The first is noticeable. The fix is to keep serving the old site while the new one builds and swap it in when it's ready. Then no request waits, but for those few seconds a page says the old commit. That changes what this plan decided, so it's Jeff's call, not something the as-built quietly does.
